title: The Business and Educational Sense of Selfless Service
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Written after a conference for online creators, this post draws three parallels between the best independent businesspeople and the best teachers. The first is that both are students of their craft, caught in a perpetual cycle of learning, teaching and making, and that submitting to the never-finished nature of the work produces credibility, which Stuart calls one of teaching's master tools. The second is joyfulness, which he presents as the necessary companion to that submission: because the work regularly fails in public, sustained practice teaches that perfectionism is folly and improvementism is the way, so failure becomes normal and even generative. The third and longest is about what you aim at. Stuart's claim is that aiming at the highest good for the people you serve produces the lower-level results as a by-product, and he works the argument through three cases, his AP world history class, his own book, and the software company that renamed itself around selfless service. The most quotable formulation is his metaphor for test scores: the test gets a seat at the back of the aeroplane but does not get to be the pilot. He closes by warning that the posture cannot be lip service.
points: The three parallels are specific rather than atmospheric: studentship of the craft, joyfulness under public failure, and aiming at other-centred results.
Credibility is identified as the mechanism by which humility pays, with submission to the never-finished nature of the work making a teacher more believable.
Perfectionism is contrasted with improvementism as the disposition that survives repeated public failure, which is what makes the joyfulness sustainable rather than performed.
The central claim is causal and counterintuitive: aim at the highest good and the conventional results arrive as a by-product, not the other way round.
The aeroplane metaphor gives the position a usable form, taking the test seriously without letting it pilot the course, and the piece closes by ruling out lip service.
quotes: It seems that the best online businesspeople have a good deal in common with the best teachers, at least in three ways.
When we humble ourselves to the “never finished” nature of teaching, it makes us better and more believable.
Experience has taught these people — like it teaches us teachers — that failure is normal, and it can even be generative for future success.
when you aim at the highest good for your audience — the best book for them, the best course, the most transformative teaching — you can get pretty great lower-level results thrown in, too.
In teaching, when we aim at the highest good of our students — their long-term flourishing by way of mastering our course material — we get the rest thrown in.
It's just that the test gets a seat in the back of the airplane — it doesn't get to be the pilot.
It can't be lip service — none of this, “We want what's best for kids” when we really just want them to score high on the state test.
